Before you start

Students look at chirping as something that can bring guys closer or keep them alone, and think about who gets the real them. Bring scraps of paper, keep the talk on situations and never on students in the room, and nobody shares the closing card.

Every student in the room

Treat chirping as something guys mostly do out of affection, and never let a slide or a joke make gay, bi or trans students the example of what guys are afraid of being called (slide 4 and the moments).

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Something like: “Today’s about chirping. Nobody’s in trouble, and I’m not here to tell you to stop. Some of the best friendships run on it.” If anyone asks: glazing is over-the-top praise, which is mostly the thing guys get roasted for. This is for everyone in the room, whatever their gender: everyone plays to some kind of audience.

Slide 2 · Notes

Students write a few words, then a few volunteers share. The next slide shows where answers usually land.

Slide 3 · Notes

Say: “So the chirp isn’t the friendship. It rides on top of something else.” That’s the idea the rest of the lesson builds on.

Slide 4 · Notes

Read both columns. The next slide asks what changes.

Slide 5 · Notes

Let them find it. The next slide names what usually comes up.

Slide 6 · Notes

Add the research quietly: teasing usually comes with signals that it’s play, and among friends it often brings people closer. It hurts when those signals drop out or one guy is always the target.

Slide 7 · Notes

Take a few guesses. The next slide shows what researchers heard.

Slide 8 · Notes

Nobody decided this. It happens one chirp at a time. Way’s research isn’t a story about one kind of guy; the loss showed up across her group. Say plainly: “There’s nothing wrong with being gay. The word gets used as a fence, and it fences in every guy.” Teacher only: in 2021, 15% of American men said they had no close friends, up from 3% in 1990.

Slide 9 · Notes

Far more young men in three countries said society expects guys to act tough and never ask for help than said they believed it themselves.

Slide 10 · Notes

Students answer to themselves or out loud; the question works for anyone, whatever their gender. Take a few answers: being scared, being sad, being excited about something nerdy, saying you missed someone, liking poetry or theater or your little sister. Don’t push for personal ones. “Chirping can be how guys keep the script running. Nobody has to say anything real, because the next joke is already coming.” If a student says toughness matters, agree: strength and holding it together for your people are real. The question is whether you ever get to put it down.

Slide 11 · Notes

Lead with the good: closeness looks different in different families, and all of it counts. Leave room for students to admire the men who raised them, and avoid “In X families” generalizations. Gay, bi, trans and questioning students are in most rooms; never let them be the example of what guys are afraid of being called.

Slide 12 · Notes

Everyone writes two things, whatever their gender. Collect, shuffle, and tally both out loud. The next slide shows what usually happens.

Slide 13 · Notes

If your tally doesn’t show the gap, say so honestly and ask why someone might keep up the act anyway.

Slide 14 · Notes

Pairs talk it through, then a few share. The question for each: what’s one small move that keeps the fun and lets him be a person? The next slide shows one good move.

Slide 15 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 16 · Notes

Pairs decide. The next slide shows one good move.

Slide 17 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 18 · Notes

Pairs decide. Close with: “You don’t have to give up chirping. Just make sure it’s not the only thing you’ve got.”

Slide 19 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 20 · Notes

Turn and talk, partners by seat. Some students, including some autistic students and students still learning English or the local slang, may find it harder to tell a chirp from an insult: “I couldn’t tell if he was joking” is a fair answer. Nobody speaks for a group.

Students write for themselves; nobody shares. Share the student page link; it has the research and some small moves to try.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can tell a chirp that brings friends closer from one that keeps them at arm's length, notice who the audience is, and name one person who gets the real them. Chirping is treated as a real part of how friends connect; nobody is told to stop.

Materials

  • Scraps of paper for the warm-up and the anonymous cards
  • Index cards or notebooks for the private closing question
  • The student page link (last slide) to share after advisory

Flow

  1. 2 minOpen: nobody's in trouble
  2. 2 minHow do you know he likes you? (written)
  3. 3 minBonds or buries
  4. 3 minWhat happens to guys' friendships
  5. 2 minThe script
  6. 3 minAnonymous cards
  7. 4 minThree moments (pairs)
  8. 1 minWho gets the real you? (private) and the student page

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Bonds or buries (3), the anonymous cards (3), one of the three moments in pairs (3), the student page link (1). The student page has the research and the small moves.

Before you teach
Don't make chirping the villain.

Most chirping is affection in disguise, and students will tune out fast if this sounds like "stop roasting each other." Say it early and mean it: "Some of the best friendships run on this." The question for the whole lesson is narrower: is it the only way you ever talk?

Keep it about situations.

Never use a real chirp from your class or a student's name, even as a joke. If a student starts telling a story about someone in the room, redirect: "Let's keep it to made-up guys today."

Expect a little chirping during the lesson.

Someone will roast a friend's answer. That's fine and kind of perfect. Laugh, then ask lightly, "Bonds or buries?" Don't make an example of anyone.

Girls and nonbinary students are part of this.

Everyone plays to some audience, and everyone has watched a friend get roasted into silence. Don't ask girls to explain what guys are like, and don't make them the audience the guys perform for.

Watch for the student who's the target.

If one student seems to be the regular punchline, or writes something on a card that sounds like real bullying or being alone, check in privately after and walk him to a counselor that day. Don't ask about it in the circle.

Respect the families.

Many families, cultures and faiths value toughness, respect and keeping private things private. That's no flaw, and plenty of students admire men who live that way. Keep the question on friendship: does every friend get only the act?

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Not only straight boys.

Gay, bi, trans and questioning students are in most rooms. "That's gay" and "no homo" are the words doing the policing in this lesson, so name them as pressure on every guy, never as a joke. No scenario turns on a gay character as the punchline. Know where to point students: a counselor and The Trevor Project (call 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678).

The research isn't about one kind of boy.

Niobe Way's boys were mostly Black, Latino and Asian American teens in New York City public schools, and they described the same loss of close friends. Say so; it keeps students from hearing this as a story about rich white kids or about one culture.

Girls and nonbinary students get the same questions.

Everyone answers the warm-up and the cards. Girls have their own versions of performing for a group (the Inner Circle lesson covers some of it). Nobody speaks for their gender.

Family, culture and faith shape how closeness shows up.

In some families affection is loud and physical, in others it's shown by showing up, fixing things or working side by side. All of that counts. Avoid "In X families" generalizations, and leave room for students to admire the men who raised them.

Not every student has a man at home, or close friends yet.

Some students are raised by moms, grandparents, two moms or in kinship care, and some are new or between friend groups. The closing question is private and "one person" can be anyone: a sibling, a cousin, a coach, a teammate, a parent.

Some students read the bit differently.

Some autistic students, and students still learning English or the local slang, may have trouble telling a chirp from an insult, and may be the target more often. Treat "I couldn't tell if he was joking" as a fair answer, not a missed cue. Let students vote with a thumb from their seat if standing or speaking up is hard.

What the research says

Psychologist Niobe Way followed boys through adolescence. In early adolescence many described best friends they shared secrets with and couldn't live without. By late adolescence many said those friendships were gone, and a common reason was not wanting to seem gay or "soft."

Way, Deep Secrets, Harvard University Press, 2011

Way's boys were mostly Black, Latino and Asian American teens from working-class and poor families in New York City public schools.

Way, 2011

Teasing usually mixes a small jab with signals that it's play: a grin, an exaggerated voice, a nickname. Among friends it often brings people closer. It hurts when those signals drop out or one person is always the target.

Keltner, Capps, Kring, Young and Heerey, Psychological Bulletin, 2001

In a survey of young men in the U.S., U.K. and Mexico, many more said society expects guys to act tough, never ask for help and hide being scared than said they believed it themselves.

Heilman, Barker and Harrison, The Man Box, Promundo, 2017

In a 2021 national survey, 15% of American men said they had no close friends, up from 3% in 1990.

Cox, Survey Center on American Life, 2021

The author bell hooks wrote that boys are pushed to cut off feelings to be accepted as men, and that the cost shows up later as loneliness.

hooks, The Will to Change, 2004
